messages.subject: Examining significant relationship between parameters for only some subsetted sites from composite MSOM
parts:
Hi all,

I am working on creating a bayesian multi-species occupancy model(s) in JagsUI where I'm testing a hypothesis examining whether habitat fragmentation has a significant impact of on species persistence (richness, and occupancy probabiltiy as measures) independent of forest cover, depending on the amount of forest cover in a given site, in sites with different levels of remnant forest cover (along a gradient 0-100% remnant forest cover). 

I have continuous forest cover variables for 55 sites, and fragmentation metrics for these sites as well. What I originally wanted to do was generate a few models, each with an interaction term between the forest cover metric and fragmentation metric, to test whether the effect of fragmentation is dependent on the amount of forest cover, for sites that have levels of forest cover falling into three different overall categories: <30%, 30-60% and >60%. So each model would just contain the sites with levels of forest cover that fall into one of those three categories, and then I would compare the models. The issue is, if I create separate models using just sites that have continuous forest cover levels corresponding to these categories, I will have very small sample sizes for my sites, and I'm afraid my models won't converge. For example, out of the 55 sites, maybe 10 of them have levels of forest cover that are <30%--so this isn't a lot of sites/species data to pull from for a hierarchical model.

What I wanted to get input on is a way I could still test the impact of the fragmentation*forest cover interaction term on species richness/occupancy probabiltiy for just sites that fall into one of those three overall categories at a time, by extracting from the full composite model (which includes all sites with all levels of forest cover and fragmentation) the posterior distributions for just those sites (e.g. just sites that fall into a 30-60% forest cover category, and the accompanying species data for just those sites) to examine the effect and signfiicance of the relationship of the forest cover*fragmentation coefficient (e.g. with plots and CRIs) and species data for just that subset of sites?  

I also spoke with Andy Royle and he suggested I create dummy variables for each of the three forest cover categories I'm looking at, and monitoring a b1 coefficient for each. I was thinking I could do this but while having each of these forest cover category coefficients have an interaction term with the fragmentation metric in the model equation, so I could test the significance/slope etc of the fragmentation metric within each of these forest cover categories (<30%, 30-60%, >60%) and its impact on occupancy probability, and compare between the different forest cover category coefficients to see if there are differences in impact/significance?

Any thoughts/input are greatly appreciated! Thank you!

Best,

Jordan

Dear Jordan,

so you have 55 sites for which you can estimate richness/occupancy as a function of forest cover and fragmentation metrics ? I don't understand why you want to fit a series of models ? Why not fit just one model and test the hypothesis that you are interested in: of an interaction between the two explanatory variables.

Conceptually, you can think of this in terms of linear model syntax as follows. You are interested in the following model: y ~ cover + fragment + cover:fragment

Here, y is your metric of community "intactness" (i.e., occupancy/species richness) and it's the interaction terms which tells you whether the effect of forest cover is dependent on forest cover (or vice versa).

Or do I misunderstand something ?

Best regards  --- Marc

parts:
Hi Marc,

Thank you for your reply! And no worries, I understood that you were implying I test the effect of forest cover dependent on fragmentation--or really I'm more interested in the opposite (whether the effect of fragmentation is dependent on the level of forest cover) but really all in the same with an interaciton term.

So yes, creating an interaction term is the direction I went in. In other similar studies (De Camargo et al., 2018, Püttker, et al., 2020--see attached if interested) they tested several models each examining sites with the level of forest cover falling into one of the low, intermediate or high forest cover level categories, and compared the findings across models. But they also had larger datasets, so I agree using an interaction term in one composite model makes the most sense for me.

The thing is, just doing an interaction term between forest cover and my fragmentation metric if I am using my full dataset with sites that have levels of forest cover across the full gradient (0-100%) won't be sufficient to test my hypotheses, as I'm trying to see if this dependence changes when examining just landscapes that have low levels of forest cover, and just landscapes that have intermediate levels of forest cover, as well as those across the full gradient. There are different hypotheses and theories about how fragmentation should behave depending on the level of total forest cover in a site, and I want to test those (e.g. see: Villard and Metzger, 2014). So in order to test for this relationship for just sites in those categories when I'm using a composite model, I believe I would need to include dummy variables as Andy Royle suggested, for sites that are considered low cover (<30% cover), and for sites that have intermediate cover (30-60%), and then create an interaction term between that dummy variable (one for low cover sites, one for intermediate level sites--so separate coefficients) and my fragmentation metric, to determine whether the effect of fragmentation is dependent on forest, or not,  at just sites with low cover, and at just sites with intermediate cover, and compare results. I'm not sure I'm explaining this very well, but hopefully that clarifies it! I'll also attach my data below.

So I have tried testing some models--I am having some convergence issues with the SDs for some parameters, and I think the model might be overparamaterized. I had originally wanted to test one fragmentation metric for intermediate forest cover sites (edge dentisty) and one for low level forest cover sites (patch density) as those metrics were found to perform better in sites with particular levels of remnant habitat cover (patch density for low level habitat sites, edge density for intermediate level). But I think to reduce complication and have a better chance the models converge I may just use one metric for fragmentation, edge density. I also was including edge density, patch density and forest cover as independent covariates in the model to see what their effect was/if it is different from the interaction terms. I also did indeed include an interaction term between my forest cover covariate and fragmentation covariate (edge density) to see if the effect of fragmentation is dependent on forest cover when examining across all levels of forest cover, as you suggested above.

If I clarified this a bit, I would appreciate feedback on the use of the dummy variables for low level forest cover sites and intermediate level forest cover sites, and of using interaction terms between those variables and the fragmentation metric, monitoring them as separate b1 coefficients. I attached my covariate/species data datasheet, and my most recent model equation below. I created separate columns for intermediate forest cover ("medfor") and low cover ("lowfor"). For the "medfor" category, for example, I placed a 0 in each row where the site has a level of forest cover that is not intermediate (not between 30-60% forest cover) and a 1 would the sites that did; ditto for the low cover sites, but placing 1s only for sites that are <30%. 

I also would appreciate some insight on how to interpret the outputs for these interaction coefficients, as it's not entirely intuitive to me how to best interpret them; e.g. whether they have a positive or negative slope, and what might suggest for the dependence of a fragmentation effect on forest cover for different levels of forest cover, or lack thereof, based on the output (beyond significant CRIs I suppose).

Thank you!!

Best,

Jordan

​Dear Jordan,

wow, this must be the longest list contribution I have ever seen 🙂 So thanks, I understand better now what you want. Of course I totally agree with Andy Royle that an indicator approach is useful here. So, distinguish your three types of sites, depending on how much forest cover they have. There are multiple ways in which you can work with these indicators, but if the forest cover class represented by these indicators is the only categorical explanatory variable in your model, then it might be easiest to set up three such indicators, one for each cover class. For instance, 'low' has ones for every site that is in the 0-30% category and zeroes for all other sites and so forth. A sketch of a linear model that will enable you to test whether the effects of fragmentation are different in three classes of forest cover would look like this:

for(i in 1:55){                     # Loop over all 55 sites
    logit(theta[i]) <- alpha1 * low[i] + beta1 * low[i] * frag[i] +    # Logit linear regression of theta on fragmentation in sites with low forest cover
                       alpha2 * medium[i] + beta2 * medium[i] * frag[i] + # Same for sites with medium forest cover
                       alpha3 * high[i] + beta3 * high[i] * frag[i]       # Same for high forest cover 
}

In this formulation, the binary indicator variables 'low', 'medium' and 'high' act like switches that turn on or off the three linear regressions (with alpha and beta) depending on which forest cover class a site belongs to. To test hypotheses about differences in the effects of fragmentation between the three forest cover classes, you can then define derived quantities as follows:

diff.beta12 <- beta1 - beta2                # Tests whether low and medium have same slope
diff.beta13 <- beta1 - beta3                # .... whether low and high have same slope
diff.beta23 <- beta2 - beta3                # ..... whether medium and high have same slope

Looking at the posterior distributions of these difference terms will let you see the evidence for differences between the slopes of logit(theta) on fragmentation between sites in the three different classes of forest cover (i.e., low, medium and high).

I do note though that all of this is really just plain old linear modeling, where you want to specify linear models with categorical and continuous explanatory variables that represent your hypotheses of interest. So stuff like you do with the R functions lm() or glm() when you write things such as lm(y ~ a*x) and the like. Just that here, (1) you have to specify these linear models in a more fundamental way rather than using the nifty formula language in these functions and (2) the linear model is not in the mean of a normal distribution assumed for the response, but inside of some more complex hierarchical model for one of its parameters. But the linear modeling principles are EXACTLY the same. That's why knowing linear modeling really well is so rich also for much more advanced statistical analyses.

Good luck and best regards  --- Marc

​Dear Jordan,

wow, this must be the longest list contribution I have ever seen 🙂 So thanks, I understand better now what you want. Of course I totally agree with Andy Royle that an indicator approach is useful here. So, distinguish your three types of sites, depending on how much forest cover they have. There are multiple ways in which you can work with these indicators, but if the forest cover class represented by these indicators is the only categorical explanatory variable in your model, then it might be easiest to set up three such indicators, one for each cover class. For instance, 'low' has ones for every site that is in the 0-30% category and zeroes for all other sites and so forth. A sketch of a linear model that will enable you to test whether the effects of fragmentation are different in three classes of forest cover would look like this:

for(i in 1:55){                     # Loop over all 55 sites
    logit(theta[i]) <- alpha1 * low[i] + beta1 * low[i] * frag[i] +    # Logit linear regression of theta on fragmentation in sites with low forest cover
                       alpha2 * medium[i] + beta2 * medium[i] * frag[i] + # Same for sites with medium forest cover
                       alpha3 * high[i] + beta3 * high[i] * frag[i]       # Same for high forest cover 
}

In this formulation, the binary indicator variables 'low', 'medium' and 'high' act like switches that turn on or off the three linear regressions (with alpha and beta) depending on which forest cover class a site belongs to. To test hypotheses about differences in the effects of fragmentation between the three forest cover classes, you can then define derived quantities as follows:

diff.beta12 <- beta1 - beta2                # Tests whether low and medium have same slope
diff.beta13 <- beta1 - beta3                # .... whether low and high have same slope
diff.beta23 <- beta2 - beta3                # ..... whether medium and high have same slope

Looking at the posterior distributions of these difference terms will let you see the evidence for differences between the slopes of logit(theta) on fragmentation between sites in the three different classes of forest cover (i.e., low, medium and high).

I do note though that all of this is really just plain old linear modeling, where you want to specify linear models with categorical and continuous explanatory variables that represent your hypotheses of interest. So stuff like you do with the R functions lm() or glm() when you write things such as lm(y ~ a*x) and the like. Just that here, (1) you have to specify these linear models in a more fundamental way rather than using the nifty formula language in these functions and (2) the linear model is not in the mean of a normal distribution assumed for the response, but inside of some more complex hierarchical model for one of its parameters. But the linear modeling principles are EXACTLY the same. That's why knowing linear modeling really well is so rich also for much more advanced statistical analyses.

Good luck and best regards  --- Marc

Hi Jordan,
(This is partly in response to your email to me, which covers the same ground.)

So there would then basically be three different intercept terms (indicated by the alphas), one for each linear regression (for each forest level category)? Yes, and also three different coefficients for fragmentation (the betas).

the difference between the logit linear regression on psi vs theta... No difference, use psi if you want (as it's occupancy, that may be preferable).

I think you'll get into an uninterpretable muddle if you include forest cover as a continuous variable as well as a categorical variable. They are likely correlated! Leave it out for now.

Including explicit correlation between the intercepts for p and psi is also going to be a muddle, so suggest giving them independent priors.

Let's go back to the firm ground of Marc's suggestion for the Ecological Model:
for(i in 1:55){                     # Loop over all 55 sites
logit(psi[i]) <- alpha1 * low[i] + beta1 * low[i] * frag[i] +
alpha2 * medium[i] + beta2 * medium[i] * frag[i] +

alpha3 * high[i] + beta3 * high[i] * frag[i]
}

If you want to generalize this to multi-species, you will need something like this:
for(k in 1:nSec){
for(i in 1:55){                     # Loop over all 55 sites

logit(psi[i,k]) <- alpha1[k] * low[i] + beta1[k] * low[i] * frag[i] + 
                     alpha2[k] * medium[i] + beta2[k] * medium[i] * frag[i] + 
                     alpha3[k] * high[i] + beta3[k] * high[i] * frag[i]
  }
  # Species level priors
  alpha1[k] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha1, tau.alpha1)
  ... same for alpha2, alpha3
  beta1[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta1, tau.beta1)
  ... same for beta2, beta3
}

Then you'll need the usual hyperpriors for the mu's and tau's. 

Regards, Mike
